warnings: Lesson is long at 4375 words; consider tightening for reading flow.
Quiz language appears sparse; make assessment prompts explicit.

improvement_notes: The lesson is unusually technically careful, but it is substantially longer than necessary for a foundational introduction. Several warnings about abstraction, safety, normalized force, and sensor uncertainty recur across multiple sections and should be consolidated.

Add an explicit early distinction between a potential-field vector field and a physical force field before introducing joules and newtons. Although the later qualification is correct, beginners may temporarily interpret the simulation coefficients as physically calibrated forces.

The attractive and repulsive equations are rigorous, but the transition from scalar potential to negative gradient would benefit from one short one-dimensional derivative example before presenting the full two-dimensional obstacle formula.

The worked robotics example explains when repulsion activates but does not numerically calculate the resulting two-dimensional repulsive and net vectors. Add one compact numerical vector calculation so the stated calculation objective is fully reinforced before the longer code lab.

The Python Lab is strong and aligned, but it is too large for many beginners to inspect effectively. Consider separating a minimal learner implementation from an annotated reference implementation, or provide staged checkpoints for attraction, repulsion, motion, and collision checking.

The code reports a collision after appending the candidate point to the path. This is logically consistent for diagnostics, but explain explicitly that the candidate is recorded to document the failed proposed motion, not because a safe controller would command it.

Add a short visual or table contrasting endpoint clearance with swept-segment clearance using one concrete obstacle-crossing example. This is one of the lesson's most important practical ideas and deserves a more immediate demonstration.

The lesson introduces local minima, oscillation, collisions, saturation, footprint inflation, noisy sensing, and layered planning. A short priority hierarchy would help beginners distinguish fundamental limitations from implementation extensions.
Accessibility would improve with a brief plain-language summary after the mathematical core and with fewer simultaneous symbols, units, and caveats in the first presentation of repulsion.
The lesson should include one explicit reflection prompt asking students to explain why a global planner plus local potential-field layer can be safer or more capable than either method alone.
